entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_scrape
entries.description:
Scrape one URL and return its content, or execute catalogued Alexandria capabilities. URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`; the `alexandria` and `requestId` parameters describe batching, retries, errors and provider terms. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

requestId.description: Identifies one logical Alexandria execution; generated when omitted and returned with the result. Repeated attempts of the identical payload require the same ID. A new ID cannot reconcile a pending or uncertain execution. A caller-supplied ID supports recovery if no response is received. Errors relay a code and may include chargeId. request_in_flight (409) means the execution is pending; request_unresolved (503) requires reconciliation under the same ID; duplicate_request (409) means the ID belongs to a different payload; unknown_provider (404), insufficient_credits (402) and billing_unavailable (503) mean nothing executed.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. nextTool identifies access to retained results without repeating a successful provider call. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. THIRD_PARTY_DATA_TERMS_REQUIRED (403) means execution is blocked by provider terms, with requiresAction.url for review by an organization admin. Through this tool, terms/show displays the agreement and terms/accept records acceptance; acceptance requires explicit user authorization for the reviewed version and digest and confirmed:true. A data request does not authorize acceptance. Provider execution remains blocked until acceptance is confirmed.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

options.description: Capability options as declared by its contract.

toolDetail.description: URL mode only: domain discovery detail, summary by default; compact returns provider/capability/description, full includes contracts. Ignored with alexandria.

domainTools.description: URL mode only: include domain-matched Alexandria tools for the page in tools on the returned document. Ignored with alexandria.

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Firecrawl__firecrawl_search
entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

1	# Review and Plan: Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation (Sportsmith)
2	
3	Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
4	Written 2026-09-25. Private working document.
5	
6	Source: Simon Harries, *The Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation* (Sportsmith). Seven parts: seven PDFs plus seven videos, about 2 h 10 min in total. Every PDF and every transcript in this folder was read. The transcripts are machine speech-to-text checked against the player captions; nobody listened back to the audio. Two terms are still unclear, Part 3 at about 15:51 and Part 6 at about 02:24. They are left unclear here too.
7	
8	## 1. What the course is
9	
10	It is one AFL practitioner's framework for the bridge from gym to field. It has three parts:
11	
12	- **Five levels.** Level 1 to Level 5, then a return to training.
13	- **Three pillars.** Linear running from submaximal to maximal velocity (MV), multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skill.
14	- **Two axes.** Intensity (competency, then capacity) and complexity (control, then chaos).
15	
16	The course ends with a four-step recipe for building your own framework: levels, pillars, intensity factors, drill menu.
17	
18	The numbers that make it worth owning come from the Part 3 transcript, because the PDF lost the table:
19	
20	| Level | Target % of max velocity | Typical content |
21	|---|---|---|

# Review and Plan: Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation (Sportsmith)

Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics
Written 2026-09-25. Private working document.

Source: Simon Harries, *The Fundamentals of On-Field Rehabilitation* (Sportsmith). Seven parts: seven PDFs plus seven videos, about 2 h 10 min in total. Every PDF and every transcript in this folder was read. The transcripts are machine speech-to-text checked against the player captions; nobody listened back to the audio. Two terms are still unclear, Part 3 at about 15:51 and Part 6 at about 02:24. They are left unclear here too.

## 1. What the course is

It is one AFL practitioner's framework for the bridge from gym to field. It has three parts:

- **Five levels.** Level 1 to Level 5, then a return to training.
- **Three pillars.** Linear running from submaximal to maximal velocity (MV), multidirectional speed and agility, and sport-specific skill.
- **Two axes.** Intensity (competency, then capacity) and complexity (control, then chaos).

The course ends with a four-step recipe for building your own framework: levels, pillars, intensity factors, drill menu.

The numbers that make it worth owning come from the Part 3 transcript, because the PDF lost the table:

| Level | Target % of max velocity | Typical content |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50–70% | Running prep drills (dribbles, A-skips, pogos, scissors); fixed-distance repeats with a time target (60 m in 13 → 12 → 11 s) |
| 2 | 70–75% | Faster 60 m repeats; COD under 45° |
| 3 | 75–85% | Broken strides: 20 m accelerate, 20 m hold, 20 m decelerate, with only the hold phase timed (e.g. 2.88–3.0 s ≈ 24–25 km/h); closed-reactive drills |
| 4 | 85–95% | Undulating sessions; flies; open-reactive drills; bigger spaces |
| 5 | >95–100% | Evasive and competitive work; repeat sprints (2 × 3–4 × 40 m, all >85% MV, one every 30 s) |

**The gate at 75–85% MV.** Before a player runs faster than this, the course checks four things:
- enough healing time;
- earlier sessions came back with minimal pain or awareness of the area;
- force benchmarks: Nordic at least 80–85% of the player's pre-injury value for hamstrings, seated calf isometric about 1.7–1.8× body weight for the calf;
- a reactive-strength hop test.

**The exit rule.** At least one, ideally two, exposures above 90% MV before return. He gives no fixed number and says it depends on context.

## 2. Objective opinion

What is strong:

1. **Session-level numbers are rare, and this course has them.** The 60 m timed repeats, the broken-stride timing, the linear-then-undulating shift at about 80–85%, the 75–85% gate, and the repeat-sprint format can all be written into a plan tomorrow. Most RTP writing stops at "progress gradually."
2. **The intensity levers are the most useful single table in the course.** For multidirectional work he names eight dials: velocity change, entry velocity, COD angle, preparation distance or time, space, reactivity, % effort, and % MV. He also points out that they interact: shrinking the space caps the entry speed. That gives you a checklist, not a feel.
3. **Intensity and complexity are separate axes.** He is explicit that a new level does not make every drill chaotic. Some actions stay controlled at high intensity while others are already in chaos. That is correct, and many practitioners get it wrong.
4. **The case studies are honest.**
   - Case 1 returned without ever exceeding 90% MV.
   - Case 2 returned a week before the staff recommendation.
   - Sprint volume was under-dosed at 40% of game value.
   - A low high-speed-running threshold (17 km/h) twice inflated the totals by accident.

   Real practice looks like this, and it shows where the framework bends.

What is weak:

1. **It is Matt Taberner's control-chaos continuum with a velocity layer added.** Harries credits Taberner himself. You already hold five Taberner papers (see `RTP_Constraints_Course/RESOURCES.md`). The course adds nothing new to the theory; its new value is the worked numbers.
2. **The complexity axis rests on older motor-learning theory, not ecological dynamics.** This matters most for Joe's course.

   - He mentions "constraints-based learning design" once, in Part 2, in one sentence, and never puts it into practice.

3. **The progression criteria are almost all physical.** Healing time, pain, force benchmarks and % MV are all measured. The one behavioural criterion ("if they hesitate… they are not ready") is stated in Part 2 and never measured. That hesitation is exactly the subjective judgement Joe says he cannot defend to objective people.
4. **AFL is not American football.** AFL is continuous: about 13 km a game and about 200 m of very-high-speed running. Football is intermittent, position-specific and built around collision. The % MV logic transfers; the thresholds do not.

- one small first piece;

- **Why first.** It turns Harries' method into Baylor numbers without changing anyone's workflow. It needs no clinical sign-off because it is a calculator, not a clearance tool. Joe asked for exactly these numbers in his tool spec ("return-to-run and high-speed running for hamstrings").
- **Size.** One script against data you already have, rendered as a one-page PDF.
- **Target.** After the three items already queued, or swapped in if it is a better ship than one of them. That is your call.

**The next three pieces, in order, one at a time:**

1. **A football version of the intensity-lever table.** Keep Harries' eight dials. Add a contact pillar with its own dials: opponent size and intent, stance and start, hand-fighting, live versus thud. Joe's `NOTES.md` already names the split: *Sarama and Gray answer what the task looks like; Taberner answers how much the athlete can take today.* **Harries belongs to the Taberner family, on the dosage side.** The two courses are not competing. Harries gives the **intensity** axis in numbers. Joe's course gives the **complexity** axis its proper theory, so that "chaos" means representative information, not random noise.

2. **Joe's tool spec.** The spec asks for research-backed numbers and for undulation with the team week. Harries supplies:
   - the linear-then-undulating pattern;
   - the 75–85% gate;
   - the ">90% MV exposures" exit rule;

   These fill the tool's numbers layer, labelled as expert heuristics.
3. **Lesson candidate, for later.** "Harries' reactivity ladder, re-read ecologically." name: ingest-review-gate
description: "Before any expensive, hard-to-inspect ingest (ingest-book atomization): a verification step plus an independent model review must pass first"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory

  originSessionId: 4597514e-1de9-4f80-87b7-4c8742ddec83
  modified: 2026-09-05T14:57:33.666Z
---

**Stated 2026-09-05**, finishing the Myszka book scan, when Eric was asked how much of the
pipeline could run on a cheaper model.

**Do not run `/ingest-book` (or any comparable atomization) straight off a freshly built
artifact. Gate it on two things: an automated verification step, and a review by an
independent model — Codex, or a fresh adversarial agent if Codex is unavailable.**

**Why:** the ingest is the expensive step *and* the one whose output is hardest to eyeball.
A page-order error costs almost nothing to make, is baked into the PDF, and is then
inherited silently by every note built from it. Eric's own framing: "cheap step, very
expensive mistake." He explicitly declined to cheapen the ingest itself, because that is
where judgement about what matters in the text happens.

**How to apply:**

- Build the artifact, then **verify by a route that shares no code path with how it was
  built.** For the book scan: the order was set by a *visual* read of cropped folio bands,
  so verification read the folio out of the *full-page OCR text* of the finished PDF, and a
  third pass rendered the PDF and read the folios off the rendered pages.
- **A cheap arithmetic identity is worth having, but do not oversell it.** `files −
  duplicates == last − first + 1` costs nothing; make it a hard gate that refuses to
  proceed, and test it with a deliberately corrupted input. **But it is a map-consistency
  check, not a proof of order.** On the default path — where folios are assigned as a
  running counter — the two sides of the identity are equal *by construction*, so the gate
  compares a number with itself. A transposition, a wrong start page, a missed duplicate,
  and two cancelling errors all pass it.
- **Audit the verification itself, not just the artifact.** The first version of
  `verify_pdf.py` "checked" that folios increase by appending the *expected* value and
  testing that those increased — true by construction, so it printed YES unconditionally.
  A check that cannot fail is worse than no check. **Prove a check can fail**: feed it a
  deliberately corrupted copy and confirm it says NO.
- **State coverage and blind spots in the output.** Six of 240 pages printed no folio and
  contributed no evidence; a uniform offset error is invisible to a folio check. Print
  that, do not imply 100%.
- Then hand it to the independent reviewer with an instruction to **falsify**, not confirm,
  and with the specific claims spelled out.

**The related cheap-model decision (same conversation):** a small model may take the first
pass at reading page numbers off contact sheets, because the sheet prints the *expected*
number beside each crop — so the job is spotting disagreements, not reading every number.
Anything it flags, and anything ambiguous, gets a careful second look. Eric chose this
mainly for speed; he was explicit that the savings are small and **the gate is the part
worth keeping.**

**What the gate actually caught, 2026-09-05.** The independent review returned **GO** on the
book PDF and **NO-GO** on the reference file shipped alongside it — which is the whole
argument for the gate in one result. It found: a verification check that was a tautology and
could never fail; an overstated claim about what the arithmetic gate proves; 7 chimeric
bibliography records welding one entry's authors to another's title; and 67 of 113 records
carrying a phantom author literally named "K". All were fixed before ingest. **The page order
was sound, and the thing shipped beside it was not** — so gate every deliverable, not just
the expensive one.

Related: [[book-scan-page-ordering]] · [[keystoneos-verification-habits]]

# Ingest Book

Turn a book into atomized, citable entries under the library subtree, grouped by domain and book, ready for the `advisor` skill.

**Library root:** `vault_library` in the selected platform config
**Paths:** canonical vault locations live in `~/.claude/skills/_shared/config.<platform>.json` (`vault_library`, `vault_root`) — load it if unsure; if a literal path here ever disagrees, the config wins.
**Extractors:** `~/.claude/skills/ingest-book/lib/extract_epub.py`, `extract_pdf.py`
Run extractors inside the context-mode sandbox (`ctx_execute`, language python) so raw book text never enters the conversation — only the atomized entries you write do.

## Model split (cost vs quality)

This skill mixes three kinds of work with very different model needs:
- **Extraction & structure mapping** (probe, chapter map, text cleanup) — deterministic
  Python in the sandbox. **Zero model tokens; model choice irrelevant.**
- **Orchestration** (searches, `_book.md` updates, dedup checks) — mechanical.
  **Haiku-tier is fine.**
- **Atomization** (Phase 2/3: distilling prose into accurate entries with correct
  mechanism-vs-claim, honest confidence, and a real "when NOT to apply") — this is where
  the advisor's entire value is created. **Run on Sonnet or stronger. Do NOT use Haiku
  for atomization** — a weak distillation becomes a permanent low-quality entry, and the
  generated output is only ~3K tokens/chapter, so quality-per-token matters far more than
  price-per-token. Cost levers that DON'T hurt quality: atomize only chapters you'll
  consult, and checkpoint + `/clear` between chapter batches (see Rules) so context
  doesn't compound across the book.

## Schema for every entry note

Filename: `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md`, `kind ∈ {principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim}`.

```yaml
---
type: library-entry
kind: principle
domain: <domain-slug>
book: <book-slug>
chapter: "N"            # or section label; "" if highlights with no location
topic: <2-5 word topic>
category: [tag, tag]
confidence: proven      # proven | supported | untested | contested
ingest-tier: full-text  # full-text | highlights | framework-only
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <Human title of the idea>

**What it is** — one tight paragraph.
**Why it works** — mechanism, not restatement.
**When to apply** — concrete triggers.
**When NOT to apply** — scope limits. (MANDATORY — never omit.)
**Example** — one concrete instance.
```

**Confidence is bounded by tier:** full-text ≤ proven; highlights ≤ supported;
framework-only ≤ untested. Set `contested` by hand when sources conflict.

## Phase 1 — Intake

1. Identify: book title, author, source type (PDF/EPUB | Kindle highlights | physical), target domain.
2. Compute `<book-slug>` = `kebab(title)--kebab(lastname)` (e.g. `supertraining--verkhoshansky`).
3. If the domain folder/`_domain.md` doesn't exist, create them (mirror the S&C `_domain.md` format).
4. Build `_book.md` chapter map:
   - EPUB/PDF: run the extractor with `--list` / `--probe` to get the chapter or page structure.
   - Physical: ask the user for the chapter list, or assemble from a verified public listing.
   Write `_book.md` (template below) with every chapter `status: pending`.

`_book.md` template:
```markdown
---
type: book-index
book: <book-slug>
title: <full title>
author: <author>
domain: <domain-slug>
ingest-tier: full-text | highlights | framework-only
source: "<file path or 'physical' or 'kindle-highlights'>"
created: <YYYY-MM-DD>
---

# <title> — ingest map

| # | Chapter | Status | Entries |
|---|---------|--------|---------|
| 0 | <title> | pending | 0 |
```

## Phase 2 — Extract (by tier)

**Full-text (PDF/EPUB):**
- First run `extract_pdf.py --probe`. If `scanned: true`, STOP the full-text path:
  tell the user the PDF is image-only, and fall back to framework-only tier (set
  `ingest-tier: framework-only`, cap confidence at untested). Never emit full-text-
  confidence entries from a scanned file.
- Work **one chapter at a time** (EPUB `--chapter N`; PDF `--pages A-B`). For each:
  extract candidate ideas → atomize per the schema → write entry notes.
- **After each chapter**, update that row in `_book.md` to `status: done` with the
  entry count. This is the resume checkpoint — never batch this update.

**Kindle highlights:**
- Parse `My Clippings.txt` or the highlights export in the sandbox. Cluster highlights
  by theme; write one entry per theme. `ingest-tier: highlights`, confidence ≤ supported.
- Attribute `chapter` from the highlight's location metadata when present, else "".

**Framework-only (physical / scanned):**
- Briefly interview the user for their takeaways. Supplement with *verified* public
  chapter summaries. Write 5–15 framework-level entries. `ingest-tier: framework-only`,
  confidence ≤ untested.

## Phase 3 — Quality gate (run before writing each batch)

- One idea per note. If an extracted point is compound, split it.
- "When NOT to apply" present and non-trivial.
- **Dedup + converge:** before writing, `memsearch search` the library for the same
  concept. If an existing entry (any book) covers it, DON'T duplicate — instead add a
  `[[wikilink]]` + one line to both notes recording the agreement, and only add a new
  note if it contributes a genuinely new angle.
- Never overwrite an existing file; on slug collision append `-2`.

## Phase 4 — Close-out

1. Set all done rows in `_book.md`; if partial, leave pending rows for next session.
2. Add the book to `_domain.md`'s `books:` list and the "Books in this domain" section.
3. Add the book-slug to the advisor persona's `books:` list (`advisors/<domain>.md`)
   if an advisor exists.
4. Run `memsearch index "<vault_library>"` using the selected platform config
   so entries are searchable immediately (don't wait for the SessionEnd hook).
5. Commit the vault using `vault_root` from the selected platform config: `git -C "<vault_root>" add Knowledge/library && git commit -m "ingest(<book-slug>): <N> entries, ch X-Y"`.
6. Report: entries by kind and confidence, links created, chapters remaining.

## Rules
- Raw book text stays in the sandbox; only atomized entries enter context/the vault.
- Resumable by design: `_book.md` is the source of truth for "where am I".
- A 300-page book is a multi-session job — stop at a chapter boundary, never mid-chapter.

# The Warm-Up Is the Lowest-Hanging Fruit

**What it is** — The authors call movement preparation **"one of the lowest hanging fruits in the American football training and practice landscape"** — a daily period, already scheduled, where the tone is set for how players are expected to behave.

Their reframe: the warm-up should **prepare the entire human movement system for the problem-solving to come.** Explicitly *not* just raising heart rate or body temperature, addressing flexibility or mobility through stretching, or **rehearsing movement patterns the coach deems important.** Instead, use the time to warm up the player's ability to:

- **perceive sensitively** — search the environment, scan for information;
- **cognize openly and intentionally** — make decisions, strategise about how to solve problems;
- **act adaptively** — with variability and adjustability;

even if carried out generally and at low intensity while players ramp up. And the tone to set first is **exploration and search, autonomy and authenticity** — without it, players will simply look to the coach to be told how to move.

The catalogue's warm-up activities show the shape: **exploratory lunges**, **loaded squat lean, shift and sway exploration**, **exploration in a circle**, **random traffic navigation and avoidance** (10–20 × 10–20 yards), and **comfort in chaos** (1v2, 1v3, 1v4).

**Why it works** — It costs no additional practice time. The period exists, it happens daily, and the change is in what happens inside it. The single highest-yield edit is stated elsewhere in the chapter: instead of running alone in a straight line, **include traffic navigation and movement in relation to another human**, so the system is perceiving-cognizing-acting from the first minute.

**When to apply** — First. If you are introducing any of this to a resistant staff, the warm-up is where to start: nobody's install time is threatened, no scheme changes, and the difference is visible within a session.

In rehabilitation the same logic applies with more force — a returning athlete's movement prep is often the *only* daily field time they have, and it is usually the most isolated work they do all week.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: reasoned, illustrated, untested — no evidence is offered that an alive warm-up improves anything, including preparedness. Two genuine cautions. The traditional aims are not wrong: raising tissue temperature and preparing for load are real, and an alive warm-up must still do them. And adding unpredictable traffic at the start of a session, before players are physiologically ready, introduces collision and change-of-direction exposure at the least prepared moment — build the aliveness in as the ramp proceeds, not at minute one.

**Example** — Two players jogging a 15-yard box, each free to move, each avoiding the other. Same duration, same intensity, same heart rate — and one of them now requires perception.

He argues that coaches often copy drills or methods without understanding their original purpose or the athlete and training context in which they were developed. He wants the course to build a problem-solving process: observe how an athlete moves in sport, identify the relevant mechanical issue or constraint, then choose and test an intervention.

He contrasts detailed weight-room measurement with what he sees as less developed observation of movement on the field. This is his coaching position, not a validation claim about any one assessment method.

Return to play is a recurring reason for this approach. Moyer says a program can restore an injured body part yet overlook the movement pattern present when the injury occurred. He proposes examining running, cutting, and throwing mechanics alongside rehabilitation and using specific exercises to support a technical change. **Practical takeaway:** Start with the sport movement and a concrete observation. Work backward to a plausible constraint, choose a targeted exercise or coaching task, then recheck the movement. =================== 02 - History Lesson - summary.md
# History Lesson — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 2. Based on the video transcript after comparison with the player captions.

Moyer traces sprint training from ancient Greek competition and early descriptions of alternating effort and recovery through later attempts to describe running mechanics. He uses this history to argue that coaches should examine where a method came from and how it was used before adopting it.

Most of the lesson examines the Soviet sports system. Moyer describes mass physical preparation through the GTO program, state sports schools, research institutes, and an athlete classification ladder tied to performance standards. He presents these as parts of a sustained national talent and training system, then connects that system to Soviet Olympic success and Cold War political goals.

Moyer pushes back on the idea that doping alone explains Soviet results. He acknowledges steroid use, while arguing that decades of organized coaching, athlete development, and research were central. That interpretation is his account of history; the lesson itself is not an independent historical evidence review.

**Coaching takeaway:** Consider the full training system behind a result. Use objective performance standards and understand the context of a method before borrowing an isolated exercise or practice.

**Transcript check:** Independent ASR and the player caption track show roughly 94% word-level agreement. Remaining differences are mostly fillers and number formatting. Historical numbers and Moyer's interpretation should be checked against the cited research before external use.

=================== 03 - Experts in Sprint Biomechanics - summary.md
# Experts in Sprint Biomechanics — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 3. Based on the video transcript after comparison with the player captions.

Moyer moves from the Soviet sports structure to the coaches and scientists who developed its training methods. He describes coaching as a specialized profession connected to formal education, research, and practice. The people discussed include Matveyev (periodization), Zatsiorsky (biomechanics and strength training), Verkhoshansky (special strength and adaptation), Bondarchuk (exercise transfer), and Bernstein (motor control).

Bernstein's ideas provide the lesson's main analytical lens. Movement has many degrees of freedom, so effective technique is not a single rigid shape repeated identically each time. Moyer distinguishes essential variables that directly affect task success from secondary features that can vary across athletes or situations. He argues that a coach should identify those essential features when observing a sprint, then choose an intervention that targets them.

**Coaching takeaway:** Analyze which movement actions matter for the sprinting task before correcting visible differences. Leave room for functional variation, and use the historical training literature as context for exercise selection.

**Transcript check:** Independent ASR and the player captions show roughly 93% word-level agreement. Several proper names are misspelled in both automatic sources and have been standardized using the course context. Some spoken historical details remain unverified.

=================== 04 - Joints and Muscles of Sprinting - summary.md
# Joints and Muscles of Sprinting — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 4. Based on the transcript checked against the player captions.

Moyer maps the main pelvic, hip, knee, and ankle actions involved in sprinting, then relates them to muscle activity across the stride. His central analogy is that muscles act like dimmer switches: their contribution rises and falls across phases rather than simply switching on or off.

He walks through how actions in stance and swing require coordinated contributions from the hamstrings, hip flexors, glutes, quadriceps, calf muscles, trunk, and stabilizers. He uses EMG findings and anatomical reasoning to discuss when these muscles may contribute to thigh recovery, preparing for contact, ground support, and push-off. He also addresses the debate over hamstring behavior in swing, arguing against treating it as purely isometric.

**Coaching takeaway:** Describe the movement and stride phase before selecting a strengthening exercise. Match the exercise's joint action, range, and timing to the specific sprinting action the coach aims to improve. EMG activity alone does not establish that an exercise will transfer to performance; that remains a coaching hypothesis to test.

**Transcript check:** Independent ASR and player captions show roughly 91% word-level agreement. The caption track repeatedly misrecognizes anatomical terms, so the clearer ASR was retained and likely term spellings were standardized. Exact wording for disputed terms still warrants an audio check before quotation.

=================== 05 - Coaching Eye - summary.md
# Coaching Eye — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 5 (23:52). Based on independent ASR checked against the player caption track.

Moyer uses Bernstein's account of movement variability and Verkhoshansky's distinction between key and secondary movements to explain what a coach should look for during a sprint. He argues that the goal is to recognize movement actions that matter to the task without requiring every athlete to look identical.

## Two levels of observation

| View | What Moyer looks for |
| --- | --- |
| Local | Knee drive after toe-off, the downward and backward swing-leg action he calls *pawback*, and ankle plantar flexion during stance and push-off. |
| Global | *Projection* (center-of-mass travel after toe-off), *switching* (coordination of thigh recovery and pawback), and *stiffness* (how the leg accepts force during contact). |

Moyer emphasizes thigh motion, especially the relationship between thigh angular velocity and speed. He cites Soviet-era reports on hip-flexor fatigue and work by Ken Clark on thigh angular velocity. He presents faster downward and backward foot motion as relevant to ground-force application, then describes the ankle and calf complex as major contributors during stance. The exact numerical force and energy shares quoted in the lecture are the instructor's cited claims; the transcript alone does not verify the underlying studies or whether those figures generalize across populations and sprint phases.

## Practical use

Start with a few full-speed views to judge projection, switching, and contact behavior. Use slow-motion video from useful angles to identify the local action that may explain an observed pattern. Compare repetitions and conditions before deciding what to train. The categories are an observation framework, not a validated injury screen or proof that a specific exercise will improve sprint speed.

**Transcript check:** Independent faster-whisper ASR and the player-generated caption track had 94.4% word-level sequence agreement. Clear name and anatomy spellings were standardized. Use the video for exact quotation or disputed research numbers.

=================== 06 - Assess - summary.md
# Assess — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 6 (22:51). Based on independent ASR checked against the player caption track.

Moyer applies the previous lesson's local actions (knee drive, pawback, ankle extension) and global views (projection, switching, stiffness) to filmed athletes. His main coaching point is to observe the action producing a position, and to account for individual build and physical qualities, instead of copying the silhouette of an elite sprinter.

## Observation checklist from the examples

| View or phase | Questions raised in the lesson |
| --- | --- |
| Side view, upright running | Where does the foot contact relative to the body? Is heel recovery very low, excessively high, or asymmetric? Is the thigh brought forward while the opposite leg moves down and back? |
| Early acceleration | How quickly does the athlete rise? Where does each foot land relative to the hips? Does the athlete show useful projection or appear to step far ahead of the body? |
| Toe-off | Is the knee slightly bent? Does the foot roll over the big toe? Does the leg or foot rotate? |
| Front/rear view, stance | Is there pronounced pelvic drop or side-to-side motion? Is there visible sinking at the ankle, knee, or hip? |

The filmed examples include a professional football player with asymmetric heel recovery, a high-school runner whom Moyer describes as landing far ahead of the body, athletes with limited projection during acceleration, and a college football player with visible pelvic motion. He notes that a wet track and flat shoes affected one recording and says he prefers multiple sprints and camera angles before reaching a conclusion. For possible projection or toe-off limitations, he proposes checking hip, ankle, foot, and toe range of motion before choosing an intervention.

**Evidence boundary:** Moyer reports that athletes in his own practice with noncontact lower-limb complaints have typically been heel strikers and suggests links between visible mechanics and injury or physical deficits. Those are his observations and hypotheses, not diagnoses or validated injury predictions. A video frame alone cannot establish the cause of pain or a strength or mobility limitation.

**Transcript check:** Independent faster-whisper ASR and the player-generated caption track had 94.1% word-level sequence agreement. A few clear names and sprint terms were standardized. Check the video before quoting exact wording.

=================== 07 - Injuries and Profiling - summary.md
# Injuries and Profiling — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 7 (18:33). Based on independent ASR checked against the player caption track.

Moyer argues that coaches and return-to-play staff should watch an athlete run, gather injury and training history, and consider the athlete's sport demands alongside gym tests. He uses hamstring injury as the main example. He discusses late-swing hamstring loading, foot contact, pelvic position, projection, and how stride mechanics may change under fatigue. His proposed link between heel striking or a long swing-leg lever and hamstring injury is explicitly presented as his own observation or theory; the lecture does not establish it as a causal screening rule.

## Acceleration profiling framework

Moyer presents J. J. Wild's four broad acceleration patterns as a way to organize large groups. The framework combines step length versus step frequency with longer flight time versus longer ground contact:

| Pattern in the lecture | Distinguishing feature |
| --- | --- |
| Bounders | Longer steps with more flight time. |
| Drivers | Longer steps with more ground contact. |
| Spinners | Higher step frequency with more ground contact. |
| Bouncers | Higher step frequency with more flight time. |

Moyer illustrates each pattern with team-sport athletes and says he uses the groups to choose a starting point for training. He aims to develop the quality an athlete appears to lack rather than move everyone into one preferred category. He also describes injury-site patterns that he attributes to the research, but the lecture alone does not verify their predictive accuracy or justify treating a quadrant as an injury-risk diagnosis.

## Practical use and limits

Record repeat sprints from relevant angles, describe the observed pattern, and compare it with the athlete's history and performance goals. Use the profile to form a training question, then measure how the athlete responds. Medical clearance and return-to-play decisions require the clinical team and appropriate testing. Injury rates, recurrence figures, fatigue mechanisms, and links between mechanics and injury are instructor claims here; they were not independently checked against the cited studies.

**Transcript check:** Independent faster-whisper ASR and the player-generated caption track had 94.2% word-level sequence agreement. Clear recognition errors were standardized. Check the video before exact quotation.

=================== 08 - Transfer of Training - summary.md
# Transfer of Training — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 8 (29:08). Based on independent ASR checked against the player caption track.

Moyer defines transfer of training as improvement in one task that carries over to another. He separates transfer of physical abilities, such as strength or power, from transfer of motor skill, such as sprint technique. He introduces positive, negative, zero, near, and far transfer, then asks coaches to judge exercises by the specific outcome and athlete rather than by how difficult an exercise feels.

## Exercise selection in his framework

| Category | Relationship to the sport action |
| --- | --- |
| General preparatory | Builds broad physical capacity without copying the competition movement. |
| Special preparatory | Uses relevant muscles or capacities but does not reproduce the sprint action. |
| Special developmental | Rehearses or loads a meaningful part of the sprint action, such as knee drive or pawback. |
| Competition exercise | Performs the whole action, possibly with altered conditions or small wearable loads. |

Drawing on Bondarchuk, Matveyev, Bernstein, and Verkhoshansky, Moyer argues that general and special work can coexist within a training period and that the balance should change with the athlete and season. He favors choosing exercises that match the key action to be improved, then varying the exercise while tracking both the physical and technical response. Examples include narrower partial squats, band-resisted thigh drive and pawback, and light wearable resistance during sprinting.

**Evidence boundary:** The lecture presents strong claims about the superiority of specific squat styles, exercise selection over intensity or volume, and wearable resistance. Its final kinetic-energy comparison between a loaded squat and a gram-scale wearable load is unclear and appears dimensionally inconsistent in the spoken explanation; it should not be used as a quantitative justification. An athlete case example reports a faster flying 10 after one month, but cannot establish that the wearable load caused the change. Treat the exercise categories as programming hypotheses to test with measured sprint outcomes and movement quality.

**Transcript check:** Independent faster-whisper ASR and the player-generated caption track had 94.3% word-level sequence agreement. Clear name spellings were standardized. Long passages around 19:13–20:37 and 20:53–22:06 are demonstration video without captioned speech. The player captions supplied a short passage near 22:25 that the local ASR omitted. Check the video before exact quotation, especially the numerical physics example.

=================== 09 - Correctives - summary.md
# Correctives — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 9 (14:20). Summarized from the independently generated ASR transcript checked against the player captions.

Moyer organizes this lesson as a troubleshooting menu for the movement qualities discussed earlier in the course: projection, stiffness/reactivity, switching, and toe-off. He starts with the observed sprint action, considers range of motion and strength constraints, and then chooses a drill, strength exercise, cue, or wearable resistance placement. The linked exercise demonstrations and the accompanying PDF are referenced in the video but were not independently reviewed here.

## Projection

For limited stride length or center-of-mass displacement, he first compares passive and active hip extension and flexion, ankle movement, and big-toe motion. In his framework, absent passive range calls for addressing that limitation; a gap between passive and active range suggests a need for strength in the available range. If range is adequate, he lists broad jumps, heavy sled sprints, short accelerations, resisted bounding, wall acceleration drills, and leaps for distance. He favors sled sprinting over sled pushing when conditions allow. Cues include pushing the ground away and imagining sprinting uphill. Strength examples include glute bridges, calf raises, isometric lunges, and banded or loaded front lunges. He describes loading the front of the thighs or calves with wearable resistance to emphasize forward projection.

## Stiffness and reactivity

Moyer looks for heel contact, unstable trunk position, excessive give through the ankle, knee, or hip, and full knee extension at toe-off. His drill options include buildup sprints, wicket runs, single-leg and pogo jumps, and depth jumps. He uses wickets as an external task constraint and an overhead PVC stick to stabilize the upper body. The strength menu includes squat variations, flywheel work, and running-specific isometrics. His preferred cues emphasize quick, snapping contact. He treats this category mainly as a strength or coordination issue and describes vest and ankle loading as resistance options.

## Switching and toe-off

He separates switching into knee drive and paw back. For low thigh lift or a long swing-leg lever, he proposes dribbles, banded bounding, wickets, switch jumps, knee-drive exercises, and hamstring PAILs and RAILs after checking relevant range. For a foot that drops straight down or lands too far in front of the hips, he lists scissor runs, bounding and marches, wickets, hamstring isometrics, hip extensions, and cues to drive the foot back and down. At toe-off he watches for knee lockout or outward foot rotation; he suggests checking ankle, big-toe, and tibial motion, then using foot and calf exercises and drills that direct force through the big toe.

**Practical takeaway:** Use the menu as a set of hypotheses tied to an observed action. Assess the proposed constraint, select one intervention, and recheck the sprint movement. The lesson presents Moyer's coaching methods; it does not establish that any individual corrective prevents injury or improves sprint performance in every athlete. One practitioner title near the end is unclear in both transcript sources.

=================== 10 - Motor Control and Learning - summary.md
# Motor Control and Learning — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 10 (24:54). Summarized from the independently generated ASR transcript checked against the player captions.

Moyer surveys several ways of thinking about motor control, including hierarchical, motor-program, dynamic-systems, and ecological approaches. His main coaching point is that the athlete, task, and intended change determine which ideas and tools are useful. He argues against adopting one theory for every athlete or treating adaptability as an answer without specifying the movement problem. He cites motor-control researcher Mark Latash and Nikolai Bernstein as influences. His descriptions of the research and of neural mechanisms are his account in the lesson, not an independent evidence review.

His running example is changing an athlete's heel contact toward a midfoot or forefoot contact. He says a long-practiced action can interfere with learning a similar new action. To make the difference perceptible, he uses an “old way, new way” exercise: explain the intended change, have the athlete perform each version, ask what each feels like in the athlete's own words, and alternate them. The coach then uses that vocabulary when giving feedback. He pairs this with specific strength exercises, resistance cords, and wearable resistance to help the athlete feel the targeted action. He stresses checking whether the action itself changes, not just delivering cues.

Moyer describes a three-stage progression:

1. **Isolate.** Practice the new action in a simple straight run, increasing speed only while the athlete can demonstrate the target movement. His example ramps from an easy jog toward full speed. He expects conscious attention and sensory comparison at this stage.
2. **Integrate.** Once the action holds at speed over repeated attempts, add one task demand at a time: arms overhead or crossed, head turned, carrying an object, then chasing or being chased. If the old pattern returns, reduce complexity and rebuild.
3. **Improvise.** Add changing directions, ball tasks, opponents, and progressively larger games so the athlete must adapt the action to a sport-like environment. Moyer frames this as a growing interaction between perception, action, and performance.

He closes by urging coaches to check results regardless of how appealing a motor-learning theory sounds. **Practical takeaway:** Define the target action and a way to observe it; teach the contrast in a simple setting, raise speed and task complexity gradually, and verify that the new action remains present in the conditions that matter. This is Moyer's proposed coaching sequence, not a demonstrated universal protocol.

=================== 11 - Results - summary.md
# Results — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 11 (12:36). Narration and captions end around 6:57, followed by silent side-by-side sprint examples. Summarized from the independently generated ASR transcript checked against the player captions and a check of the later visual footage. The reported measurements below come from the narration.

Moyer presents before-and-after examples to show how he evaluates his sprint coaching. He uses video and motion-analysis software to communicate changes to athletes, parents, and coaches, but says the software scores do not determine his intervention. He first watches the movement and identifies the technical action he wants to change. In particular, he cautions that a low “reactivity” score may reflect where the foot lands and how the swing leg retracts, not just the athlete's stiffness capacity.

In one high school football example, about six weeks separate the two videos. Moyer says he targeted weak projection and soft ground contacts with plyometric work focused on the ankle and calf, single-leg calf raises, and heavy sled work. He reports visible improvement in projection while saying stiffness still needs work.

For a college wide receiver, he reports that the first 10-yard split moved from 1.25 to 1.15 seconds and the second 10-yard split from 1.73 to 1.63 seconds over roughly six weeks, for a reported 0.20-second change across the 20 yards. He also shows a high school sprinter for whom he says the emphasis was calf work and swing-leg retraction, without a major change in heavy sled or squat work. In a professional athlete example, he describes a long swing-leg lever and poor switching. After PAILs and RAILs, wearable resistance, and wicket runs, he reports a video-measured angle moving from 66.6° to 45°.

**Practical takeaway:** Pair a clearly described movement target with comparable video and a relevant performance measure. These are Moyer's case examples with multiple concurrent training changes. The lesson does not isolate which exercise caused the observed changes or establish how broadly they generalize. The Results lesson was checked against its own caption and ASR transcript and is distinct from the preceding Motor Control and Learning lesson.

=================== 12 - Technique Analysis - summary.md
# Technique Analysis — summary

**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 12 (4:40). Summarized from the independently generated ASR transcript checked against the player captions.

Moyer defines technique analysis as a practical combination of biomechanics and kinesiology. He distinguishes numerical descriptions of movement from observing the sequence of key force-producing actions and the muscles involved. For his coaching purposes, that qualitative view helps answer what to change in training. He argues that if the aim is better movement on the field, the movement itself should be examined.

The lesson is largely the account of how he became interested in this approach. While working with a high school football team and an orthopedic practice in 2010, he saw a quarterback sustain an elbow fracture while throwing. Moyer describes heavy prior throwing volume and mechanics he believed were poor. Following surgery and rehabilitation, he sought help from biomechanist Dr. Michael Yessis through his mentor Mike Yosef Johnson. Moyer says Yessis reviewed earlier video, identified problems in the athlete's movement sequence, and then taught running, cutting, and throwing drills with specific strength exercises. Moyer describes that visit as the start of a long apprenticeship and a central influence on this course.

**Practical takeaway:** Examine the sport action and its sequence, then connect a concrete observation to a coaching exercise or task and reassess the action. This is Moyer's account of one athlete and his own education. The transcript sources do not make the exact elbow fracture term clear, and the story alone cannot establish that the movement pattern caused the injury or that changing it prevents recurrence.

The people discussed include Matveyev (periodization), Zatsiorsky (biomechanics and strength training), Verkhoshansky (special strength and adaptation), Bondarchuk (exercise transfer), and Bernstein (motor control).
37	
38	Bernstein's ideas provide the lesson's main analytical lens. Movement has many degrees of freedom, so effective technique is not a single rigid shape repeated identically each time. Moyer distinguishes essential variables that directly affect task success from secondary features that can vary across athletes or situations. He argues that a coach should identify those essential features when observing a sprint, then choose an intervention that targets them.
39	
40	**Coaching takeaway:** Analyze which movement actions matter for the sprinting task before correcting visible differences. Leave room for functional variation, and use the historical training literature as context for exercise selection.

46	
47	**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 4. Based on the transcript checked against the player captions.
48	
49	Moyer maps the main pelvic, hip, knee, and ankle actions involved in sprinting, then relates them to muscle activity across the stride. His central analogy is that muscles act like dimmer switches: their contribution rises and falls across phases rather than simply switching on or off.
50

He also addresses the debate over hamstring behavior in swing, arguing against treating it as purely isometric.
52	
53	**Coaching takeaway:** Describe the movement and stride phase before selecting a strengthening exercise. Match the exercise's joint action, range, and timing to the specific sprinting action the coach aims to improve. EMG activity alone does not establish that an exercise will transfer to performance; that remains a coaching hypothesis to test.

58	# Coaching Eye — summary
59	
60	**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 5 (23:52). Based on independent ASR checked against the player caption track.
61	
62	Moyer uses Bernstein's account of movement variability and Verkhoshansky's distinction between key and secondary movements to explain what a coach should look for during a sprint. He argues that the goal is to recognize movement actions that matter to the task without requiring every athlete to look identical.
63	
64	## Two levels of observation
65	
66	| View | What Moyer looks for |
67	| --- | --- |
68	| Local | Knee drive after toe-off, the downward and backward swing-leg action he calls *pawback*, and ankle plantar flexion during stance and push-off. |
69	| Global | *Projection* (center-of-mass travel after toe-off), *switching* (coordination of thigh recovery and pawback), and *stiffness* (how the leg accepts force during contact). |
70	
71	Moyer emphasizes thigh motion, especially the relationship between thigh angular velocity and speed. He cites Soviet-era reports on hip-flexor fatigue and work by Ken Clark on thigh angular velocity. He presents faster downward and backward foot motion as relevant to ground-force application, then describes the ankle and calf complex as major contributors during stance. The exact numerical force and energy shares quoted in the lecture are the instructor's cited claims; the transcript alone does not verify the underlying studies or whether those figures generalize across populations and sprint phases.
72	
73	## Practical use
74	
75	Start with a few full-speed views to judge projection, switching, and contact behavior. Use slow-motion video from useful angles to identify the local action that may explain an observed pattern. Compare repetitions and conditions before deciding what to train. The categories are an observation framework, not a validated injury screen or proof that a specific exercise will improve sprint speed.
76

80	# Assess — summary
81	
82	**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 6 (22:51). Based on independent ASR checked against the player caption track.
83	
84	Moyer applies the previous lesson's local actions (knee drive, pawback, ankle extension) and global views (projection, switching, stiffness) to filmed athletes. His main coaching point is to observe the action producing a position, and to account for individual build and physical qualities, instead of copying the silhouette of an elite sprinter.
85	
86	## Observation checklist from the examples
87	
88	| View or phase | Questions raised in the lesson |
89	| --- | --- |
90	| Side view, upright running | Where does the foot contact relative to the body? Is heel recovery very low, excessively high, or asymmetric? Is the thigh brought forward while the opposite leg moves down and back? |
91	| Early acceleration | How quickly does the athlete rise? Where does each foot land relative to the hips? Does the athlete show useful projection or appear to step far ahead of the body? |
92	| Toe-off | Is the knee slightly bent? Does the foot roll over the big toe? Does the leg or foot rotate? |
93	| Front/rear view, stance | Is there pronounced pelvic drop or side-to-side motion? Is there visible sinking at the ankle, knee, or hip? |
94	
95	The filmed examples include a professional football player with asymmetric heel recovery, a high-school runner whom Moyer describes as landing far ahead of the body, athletes with limited projection during acceleration, and a college football player with visible pelvic motion. He notes that a wet track and flat shoes affected one recording and says he prefers multiple sprints and camera angles before reaching a conclusion. For possible projection or toe-off limitations, he proposes checking hip, ankle, foot, and toe range of motion before choosing an intervention.
96	
97	**Evidence boundary:** Moyer reports that athletes in his own practice with noncontact lower-limb complaints have typically been heel strikers and suggests links between visible mechanics and injury or physical deficits. Those are his observations and hypotheses, not diagnoses or validated injury predictions. A video frame alone cannot establish the cause of pain or a strength or mobility limitation.

101	=================== 07 - Injuries and Profiling - summary.md
102	# Injuries and Profiling — summary
103	
104	**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 7 (18:33). Based on independent ASR checked against the player caption track.
105	
106	Moyer argues that coaches and return-to-play staff should watch an athlete run, gather injury and training history, and consider the athlete's sport demands alongside gym tests. He uses hamstring injury as the main example. He discusses late-swing hamstring loading, foot contact, pelvic position, projection, and how stride mechanics may change under fatigue. His proposed link between heel striking or a long swing-leg lever and hamstring injury is explicitly presented as his own observation or theory; the lecture does not establish it as a causal screening rule.
107	
108	## Acceleration profiling framework
109	
110	Moyer presents J. J. Wild's four broad acceleration patterns as a way to organize large groups. The framework combines step length versus step frequency with longer flight time versus longer ground contact:
111	
112	| Pattern in the lecture | Distinguishing feature |
113	| --- | --- |
114	| Bounders | Longer steps with more flight time. |
115	| Drivers | Longer steps with more ground contact. |
116	| Spinners | Higher step frequency with more ground contact. |
117	| Bouncers | Higher step frequency with more flight time. |
118	
119	Moyer illustrates each pattern with team-sport athletes and says he uses the groups to choose a starting point for training. He aims to develop the quality an athlete appears to lack rather than move everyone into one preferred category. He also describes injury-site patterns that he attributes to the research, but the lecture alone does not verify their predictive accuracy or justify treating a quadrant as an injury-risk diagnosis.
120	
121	## Practical use and limits
122	
123	Record repeat sprints from relevant angles, describe the observed pattern, and compare it with the athlete's history and performance goals. Use the profile to form a training question, then measure how the athlete responds. Medical clearance and return-to-play decisions require the clinical team and appropriate testing. Injury rates, recurrence figures, fatigue mechanisms, and links between mechanics and injury are instructor claims here; they were not independently checked against the cited studies.
124	
125	**Transcript check:** Independent faster-whisper ASR and the player-generated caption track had 94.2% word-level sequence agreement. Clear recognition errors were standardized. Check the video before exact quotation.

127	=================== 08 - Transfer of Training - summary.md
128	# Transfer of Training — summary
129	
130	**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 8 (29:08). Based on independent ASR checked against the player caption track.
131	
132	Moyer defines transfer of training as improvement in one task that carries over to another. He separates transfer of physical abilities, such as strength or power, from transfer of motor skill, such as sprint technique. He introduces positive, negative, zero, near, and far transfer, then asks coaches to judge exercises by the specific outcome and athlete rather than by how difficult an exercise feels.
133	
134	## Exercise selection in his framework
135	
136	| Category | Relationship to the sport action |
137	| --- | --- |
138	| General preparatory | Builds broad physical capacity without copying the competition movement. |
139	| Special preparatory | Uses relevant muscles or capacities but does not reproduce the sprint action. |
140	| Special developmental | Rehearses or loads a meaningful part of the sprint action, such as knee drive or pawback. |
141	| Competition exercise | Performs the whole action, possibly with altered conditions or small wearable loads. |
142	
143	Drawing on Bondarchuk, Matveyev, Bernstein, and Verkhoshansky, Moyer argues that general and special work can coexist within a training period and that the balance should change with the athlete and season. He favors choosing exercises that match the key action to be improved, then varying the exercise while tracking both the physical and technical response. Examples include narrower partial squats, band-resisted thigh drive and pawback, and light wearable resistance during sprinting.
144	
145	**Evidence boundary:** The lecture presents strong claims about the superiority of specific squat styles, exercise selection over intensity or volume, and wearable resistance. Its final kinetic-energy comparison between a loaded squat and a gram-scale wearable load is unclear and appears dimensionally inconsistent in the spoken explanation; it should not be used as a quantitative justification. An athlete case example reports a faster flying 10 after one month, but cannot establish that the wearable load caused the change. Treat the exercise categories as programming hypotheses to test with measured sprint outcomes and movement quality.
146	
147	**Transcript check:** Independent faster-whisper ASR and the player-generated caption track had 94.3% word-level sequence agreement. Clear name spellings were standardized. Long passages around 19:13–20:37 and 20:53–22:06 are demonstration video without captioned speech. The player captions supplied a short passage near 22:25 that the local ASR omitted. Check the video before exact quotation, especially the numerical physics example.

149	=================== 09 - Correctives - summary.md
150	# Correctives — summary
151	
152	**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 9 (14:20). Summarized from the independently generated ASR transcript checked against the player captions.
153	
154	Moyer organizes this lesson as a troubleshooting menu for the movement qualities discussed earlier in the course: projection, stiffness/reactivity, switching, and toe-off. He starts with the observed sprint action, considers range of motion and strength constraints, and then chooses a drill, strength exercise, cue, or wearable resistance placement. The linked exercise demonstrations and the accompanying PDF are referenced in the video but were not independently reviewed here.
155	
156	## Projection
157	
158	For limited stride length or center-of-mass displacement, he first compares passive and active hip extension and flexion, ankle movement, and big-toe motion. In his framework, absent passive range calls for addressing that limitation; a gap between passive and active range suggests a need for strength in the available range. If range is adequate, he lists broad jumps, heavy sled sprints, short accelerations, resisted bounding, wall acceleration drills, and leaps for distance. He favors sled sprinting over sled pushing when conditions allow. Cues include pushing the ground away and imagining sprinting uphill. Strength examples include glute bridges, calf raises, isometric lunges, and banded or loaded front lunges. He describes loading the front of the thighs or calves with wearable resistance to emphasize forward projection.
159	
160	## Stiffness and reactivity
161	
162	Moyer looks for heel contact, unstable trunk position, excessive give through the ankle, knee, or hip, and full knee extension at toe-off. His drill options include buildup sprints, wicket runs, single-leg and pogo jumps, and depth jumps. He uses wickets as an external task constraint and an overhead PVC stick to stabilize the upper body. The strength menu includes squat variations, flywheel work, and running-specific isometrics. His preferred cues emphasize quick, snapping contact. He treats this category mainly as a strength or coordination issue and describes vest and ankle loading as resistance options.
163	
164	## Switching and toe-off
165	
166	He separates switching into knee drive and paw back. For low thigh lift or a long swing-leg lever, he proposes dribbles, banded bounding, wickets, switch jumps, knee-drive exercises, and hamstring PAILs and RAILs after checking relevant range. For a foot that drops straight down or lands too far in front of the hips, he lists scissor runs, bounding and marches, wickets, hamstring isometrics, hip extensions, and cues to drive the foot back and down. At toe-off he watches for knee lockout or outward foot rotation; he suggests checking ankle, big-toe, and tibial motion, then using foot and calf exercises and drills that direct force through the big toe.
167	
168	**Practical takeaway:** Use the menu as a set of hypotheses tied to an observed action. Assess the proposed constraint, select one intervention, and recheck the sprint movement. The lesson presents Moyer's coaching methods; it does not establish that any individual corrective prevents injury or improves sprint performance in every athlete. One practitioner title near the end is unclear in both transcript sources.

170	=================== 10 - Motor Control and Learning - summary.md
171	# Motor Control and Learning — summary
172	
173	**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 10 (24:54). Summarized from the independently generated ASR transcript checked against the player captions.
174	
175	Moyer surveys several ways of thinking about motor control, including hierarchical, motor-program, dynamic-systems, and ecological approaches. His main coaching point is that the athlete, task, and intended change determine which ideas and tools are useful. He argues against adopting one theory for every athlete or treating adaptability as an answer without specifying the movement problem. He cites motor-control researcher Mark Latash and Nikolai Bernstein as influences. His descriptions of the research and of neural mechanisms are his account in the lesson, not an independent evidence review.
176	
177	His running example is changing an athlete's heel contact toward a midfoot or forefoot contact. He says a long-practiced action can interfere with learning a similar new action. To make the difference perceptible, he uses an “old way, new way” exercise: explain the intended change, have the athlete perform each version, ask what each feels like in the athlete's own words, and alternate them. The coach then uses that vocabulary when giving feedback. He pairs this with specific strength exercises, resistance cords, and wearable resistance to help the athlete feel the targeted action. He stresses checking whether the action itself changes, not just delivering cues.
178	
179	Moyer describes a three-stage progression:
180	
181	1. **Isolate.** Practice the new action in a simple straight run, increasing speed only while the athlete can demonstrate the target movement. His example ramps from an easy jog toward full speed. He expects conscious attention and sensory comparison at this stage.
182	2. **Integrate.** Once the action holds at speed over repeated attempts, add one task demand at a time: arms overhead or crossed, head turned, carrying an object, then chasing or being chased. If the old pattern returns, reduce complexity and rebuild.
183	3. **Improvise.** Add changing directions, ball tasks, opponents, and progressively larger games so the athlete must adapt the action to a sport-like environment. Moyer frames this as a growing interaction between perception, action, and performance.
184	
185	He closes by urging coaches to check results regardless of how appealing a motor-learning theory sounds. **Practical takeaway:** Define the target action and a way to observe it; teach the contrast in a simple setting, raise speed and task complexity gradually, and verify that the new action remains present in the conditions that matter. This is Moyer's proposed coaching sequence, not a demonstrated universal protocol.
186	
187	=================== 11 - Results - summary.md
188	# Results — summary
189	
190	**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 11 (12:36). Narration and captions end around 6:57, followed by silent side-by-side sprint examples. Summarized from the independently generated ASR transcript checked against the player captions and a check of the later visual footage. The reported measurements below come from the narration.
191	
192	Moyer presents before-and-after examples to show how he evaluates his sprint coaching. He uses video and motion-analysis software to communicate changes to athletes, parents, and coaches, but says the software scores do not determine his intervention. He first watches the movement and identifies the technical action he wants to change. In particular, he cautions that a low “reactivity” score may reflect where the foot lands and how the swing leg retracts, not just the athlete's stiffness capacity.
193	
194	In one high school football example, about six weeks separate the two videos. Moyer says he targeted weak projection and soft ground contacts with plyometric work focused on the ankle and calf, single-leg calf raises, and heavy sled work. He reports visible improvement in projection while saying stiffness still needs work.
195	
196	For a college wide receiver, he reports that the first 10-yard split moved from 1.25 to 1.15 seconds and the second 10-yard split from 1.73 to 1.63 seconds over roughly six weeks, for a reported 0.20-second change across the 20 yards. He also shows a high school sprinter for whom he says the emphasis was calf work and swing-leg retraction, without a major change in heavy sled or squat work. In a professional athlete example, he describes a long swing-leg lever and poor switching. After PAILs and RAILs, wearable resistance, and wicket runs, he reports a video-measured angle moving from 66.6° to 45°.
197	
198	**Practical takeaway:** Pair a clearly described movement target with comparable video and a relevant performance measure. These are Moyer's case examples with multiple concurrent training changes. The lesson does not isolate which exercise caused the observed changes or establish how broadly they generalize. The Results lesson was checked against its own caption and ASR transcript and is distinct from the preceding Motor Control and Learning lesson.

201	# Technique Analysis — summary
202	
203	**Source:** Jeff Moyer, *Fundamentals of Sprinting*, Lesson 12 (4:40). Summarized from the independently generated ASR transcript checked against the player captions.
204	
205	Moyer defines technique analysis as a practical combination of biomechanics and kinesiology. He distinguishes numerical descriptions of movement from observing the sequence of key force-producing actions and the muscles involved. For his coaching purposes, that qualitative view helps answer what to change in training. He argues that if the aim is better movement on the field, the movement itself should be examined.
206	
207	The lesson is largely the account of how he became interested in this approach. While working with a high school football team and an orthopedic practice in 2010, he saw a quarterback sustain an elbow fracture while throwing. Moyer describes heavy prior throwing volume and mechanics he believed were poor. Following surgery and rehabilitation, he sought help from biomechanist Dr. Michael Yessis through his mentor Mike Yosef Johnson. Moyer says Yessis reviewed earlier video, identified problems in the athlete's movement sequence, and then taught running, cutting, and throwing drills with specific strength exercises. Moyer describes that visit as the start of a long apprenticeship and a central influence on this course.
208	
209	**Practical takeaway:** Examine the sport action and its sequence, then connect a concrete observation to a coaching exercise or task and reassess the action. This is Moyer's account of one athlete and his own education. The transcript sources do not make the exact elbow fracture term clear, and the story alone cannot establish that the movement pattern caused the injury or that changing it prevents recurrence.
